This is a classic intro to feminism text. You can buy the book on Amazon. Here's a summary of what I get out of the intro and chapter 1.

The introduction opens up with the author's experience with other people's idea of feminism. People tend to think of feminism as man-hating, and a cause of societal ills. Feminists go against nature, feminists take all the jobs, feminists are out to keep men down. But most of these people have never actually met a feminist, and their information is third-hand.

So what is feminism? "Feminism is a movement to end sexism, sexist exploitation, and oppression."

What is the patriarchy? "Another way of naming the institutionalized sexism." The patriarchy may be supported by men and women alike.

What is feminism not? "It would be naive and wrongminded for feminist thinkers to see the movement as simplistically being for women and against men."

She goes on to say that men do benefit the most from the patriarchy, because of the assumption that they are superior to women and should rule. "These benefits come at a price." Most men do not like perpetuating the cycle of violence and domination over women. The problem is that most men don't want to lose the benefits associated with patriarchy.

Chapter 1

She starts off by rehashing the definition of feminism given in the intro. "Masses of people think that feminism is ... only about women seeking to be equal to men. And a huge majority ... think feminism is anti-male." This is a misunderstanding, because feminism is about fighting all sexist oppression, including when men are harmed by the patriarchy.

Early feminists came about after working in anti-classist and anti-racist settings. The men in these groups would speak about freedom, while continuing to subordinate the women. Most of these early feminists were white women.

When feminism progressed, it was realized that men weren't the only ones who support sexist thinking and behavior, and that women can be sexist as well. Therefore the movement changed to fight sexism in general, rather than exist as a strictly pro-women movement. It was found that a "sisterhood" that ignored issues of class and race would not be effective at fighting sexism either.

From its inception feminism was polarized. Reformists wanted to emphasize gender equality. Revolutionaries wanted to transform the entire system to bring an end to patriarchy and sexism. The reformist view got most of the coverage in the mass media. This is why there is a popular view of feminism as "women's liberation", where women just wanted what men have.

Early feminism has an intersection with racism. White men were more willing to consider women's rights if granting those rights could maintain white supremacy. Reformist feminists (mostly privileged white women) stopped even considering revolutionary feminist ideas. Ironically, it was the revolutionary feminist ideas that were most accepted in academic circles. This is another reason of the popular misconception of feminism: the revolutionary feminist theory progressed in a way that wasn't always accessible to the public.

A later development was "lifestyle feminism". This is the idea that there are as many versions of feminism as there are women. You could adhere to any politics you like and still call yourself a feminist. Take for example abortion. "If feminism is a movement to end sexist oppression, and depriving females of reproduction is a form of oppression, then one cannot be anti-choice and feminist." And yet women can insist that they are both.

This erosion of clear definitions has caused feminist politics to lose its momentum. That's why we need to share the real meaning of feminism, which is a movement to end sexist oppression.
